questions.title: Sequence after two passes of quicksort
questions.statement:
Consider an unsorted list of 8 elements given below:

`23 61 73 82 9 43 11 3`

What will be the sequence after two passes of quick sort if the first element of the list is chosen as pivot always and the list is sorted in ascending order?

**Note:** Both left and right recursive calls are made together.
questions.explanation: Pass 1 (Hoare-style partition, pivot 23): swap 61<->3, 73<->11, 82<->9, then place pivot -> 9 3 11 23 82 43 73 61. Pass 2 sorts the left part 9 3 11 -> 3 9 11, giving 3 9 11 23 82 43 73 61. Strictly, partitioning the right part with pivot 82 as well would give 3 9 11 23 61 43 73 82, which is not an option. The intended key appears to treat pass 2 as changing only the left part.

questions.title: Invalid logical address in segmentation
questions.statement:
Consider the given segment map table along with the logical addresses for the corresponding segments.

| Segment | Base | Length |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 90 | 600 |
| 1 | 1992 | 14 |
| 2 | 569 | 256 |
| 3 | 2669 | 123 |
| 4 | 912 | 569 |

Consider the following logical addresses: (0, 430), (1, 236), (2, 200), (4, 100). Which request is invalid?
questions.explanation: A logical address (s, d) is valid only if offset d < length of segment s. Segment 1 has length 14 and 236 >= 14, so it traps. The others: 430<600, 200<256, 100<569.

questions.statement: What is one of the main benefits of using the Shadow DOM in web components?
options: It allows CSS styles to be scoped to the component, preventing style leakage.
It ensures that all elements are displayed with equal padding.
It automatically optimizes the performance of your web page.
It provides built-in animations for elements.
questions.answer: It allows CSS styles to be scoped to the component, preventing style leakage.
questions.explanation: Shadow DOM encapsulates a component's DOM subtree and styles, so styles inside don't leak out and page styles don't bleed in.

questions.pattern: boolean expression simplification with De Morgan
questions.title: Reduce (ABC)' + (A'B'C)'
questions.statement:
Which one of the given options is the correct reduced expression for the given expression?

$(ABC)' + (A'B'C)' = ?$
questions.answer: As written the expression equals 1 (none of the options); the candidate selected C'
questions.explanation: By De Morgan, $(ABC)' = A'+B'+C'$ and $(A'B'C)' = A+B+C'$. Their OR contains $A + A' = 1$, so the expression is 1. If the intended expression was the product $(ABC)'(A'B'C)'$, it reduces to $C' + A'B + AB'$, which is still not listed. The question is probably mis-typed.

questions.pattern: cube net folding - which cubes can be formed
questions.title: Boxes formed by folding a net
questions.statement:
The figure marked (X) has been folded to produce different box patterns. Four boxes are given below, marked (1), (2), (3) and (4). Choose the correct alternative which indicates the boxes that are produced by folding figure (X).

**Net (X)** (described): a vertical column of four squares, from top to bottom: a face with 4 black dots; a solid black face with 3 white dots; a face with 5 black dots; a face with diagonal hatching. A blank face is attached to the left of the 5-dot face, and a face with 3 small circles is attached to the right of the hatched face.

**Boxes** (top / front / right):
1. hatched / 4 dots / blank
2. hatched / 5 dots / black
3. hatched / 3 circles / blank
4. black / 4 dots / blank
questions.explanation: Opposite pairs: 4-dot and 5-dot, black and hatched, blank and circles. That rules out (2) (hatched next to black) and (3) (circles next to blank). Folding with the 5-dot face in front gives top = black, bottom = hatched, left = blank, right = circles, back = 4-dot. With hatched on top and 4-dot in front, the right face must be circles, so (1) fails. Rotating 180 degrees about the vertical axis gives front = 4-dot, top = black, right = blank, which is (4).

questions.pattern: level sum in array-represented complete binary tree
questions.title: Sum of elements at a given level of an almost complete binary tree
questions.statement:
You are given a list A of N integers. Construct the almost complete binary tree from them and write a program to print the sum S of all the elements present in the given level.

If the elements of the list L are $[x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{10}]$, the constructed almost complete binary tree is built level by level: $x_1$ is the root; $x_2, x_3$ are its children; $x_4, x_5$ are children of $x_2$; $x_6, x_7$ are children of $x_3$; $x_8, x_9$ are children of $x_4$; $x_{10}$ is the left child of $x_5$.

An almost complete binary tree satisfies the following conditions:
1. Insertion of nodes takes place level by level, and all the nodes must be left-justified.
2. All levels from 1 to h-1 (h = number of levels) are completely filled without any gap.

Read the input from STDIN and print the output to STDOUT.
questions.input_format: The first line of input contains N, the total number of elements in the list A. (Remaining input lines cropped; presumably the N elements followed by the level number.)
questions.explanation: In level-order (array) form, level k (1-indexed) holds positions $2^{k-1}$ to $\min(2^k - 1, N)$. Sum that slice. If the level doesn't exist, handle it per the (unseen) spec. O(N) time, O(1) extra space.

questions.pattern: count minimal selections with at least V in every window of C
questions.title: Meet & Greet - ways to visit houses
questions.statement:
"Meeting people frequently is the surest way to get re-elected," advised the party President. Margaret, one of the party's elected representatives, took the advice seriously and went on a tour of her constituency. One day she came across a street with N houses. Instead of visiting every house, which would take a lot of time, she decided to visit at least V out of each C consecutive houses on the street.

Before starting off, she wonders if there are multiple ways to select the houses for this 'meet & greet'. Write a program to help Margaret find how many different ways she can visit the houses. As the number can be exponentially huge, return it modulo $10^9+7$.
questions.input_format: A single line of input contains three space-separated integers N, C and V.
questions.output_format: A single integer denoting the possible number of ways to visit the houses, modulo $10^9+7$.

examples.explanation: N = 4, C = 2, V = 1. From 4 houses, Margaret wants to visit at least 1 house from each 2 consecutive houses. There are 3 different ways (visited houses marked 1): 1010, 0110, and a third that is cropped (presumably 0101).

questions.explanation: The sample (3, not the 8 binary strings with no '00') implies only selections with the minimum possible number of visited houses are counted: for 4 2 1 these are 1010, 0101 and 0110. The minimum count is $\lfloor N/C \rfloor V + \max(0, (N \bmod C) - (C - V))$. Optimal selections have a near-periodic structure with period C, so the count can be derived combinatorially (choose block patterns and the slack positions), using fast exponentiation or a closed form because N is up to $10^9$.
